results.answer:
A measure family is a governed analytical family that carries one semantic identity and a declared family law [S7]. It is the thing named by a canonical family name like revenue and identified by a Family ID; the family law specifies how its measures are allowed to relate across anchors [S7].

Relation to measures. In Version 6, a measure is simply the family at one anchor, written F@A. For example: revenue @ transaction, revenue @ day, revenue @ {store, month}. The family name answers what analytical quantity this is; the anchor answers where it lives analytically [S2].

Family law and anchors. Measures in one family can be related by the family’s law. For example, under an additive law, revenue @ {store, month} may lawfully reduce to revenue @ store or revenue @ month. But being in the same family does not mean every anchor is reachable from every other; some anchors (e.g., week vs month) may be incomparable partitions for that family [S3].

Role in the architecture. The measure family is the basic algebraic unit in which the Theory of Data proves staging invariance and path coherence; families are nodes in the governed analytical lineage graph, and family‑establishing derivations connect them directionally. Local algebraic coherence lives inside a family; governed ancestry and identity live in the lineage graph [S6].

Terminology. Version 6 renames what Version 5 called a “measure” to “measure family,” and retires the term “member.” What V5 called a “member” is now simply a “measure” (family @ anchor), e.g., revenue@month [S5].

In short: the measure family is the governed unit that defines one analytical quantity and its lawful cross‑anchor behavior; a measure is that family at a specific anchor, F@A [S7][S2].

results.answer:
An anchor is the governed coordinate system that locates analysis in a universe. Formally, it is a complete governed partition of the universe’s root points; each block of that partition is an anchor point, so anchors are stronger than ad‑hoc “group by” labels (for example, store or {store, day} partitions the universe into those governed blocks) [S1]. Equivalently, an anchor is a typed coordinate schema built by choosing one declared level on each axis; its anchor points are the typed locations in the product of those levels (e.g., a point like “Patient 17, Visit 4, Assay A” is one such typed location) [S5][S2].

How anchors relate:
- Coarsening between anchors is admitted exactly when each chosen level is coarser along its axis hierarchy; with tree-structured axis hierarchies this makes the anchor category thin (at most one admitted coarsening between two anchors) [S2].

How anchors are used with measures:
- A measure lives at one current analytical anchor; the anchor says where that measure exists [S8].
- In the public vocabulary, a concrete measure is a measure family at one anchor: Measure = MeasureFamily @ Anchor [S3].

Examples:
- Anchor = store partitions root points by store; anchor = {store, day} partitions by each governed store–day block [S1].
- A biomedical anchor might choose levels Patient, Visit, Assay; an anchor point is one typed Patient–Visit–Assay location [S5].

results.q: How does Columna compare with dbt MetricFlow?
results.answer:
Short answer
They sit at different layers. dbt’s MetricFlow belongs to the family of semantic‑layer systems for shared metrics, joins, aggregate planning, and metric reuse. Columna/Frame‑QL is designed above that layer: it lets you declare the analytical result you want, resolves it inside a governed environment, and treats the outcome as a candidate for certification under explicit type/structure/boundary/execution premises. In other words, MetricFlow manufactures metrics; Columna governs, adjudicates, and can certify analytical results. They are complementary rather than substitutes [S1][S5][S6].

How they differ, concretely
- Purpose and scope
  - MetricFlow (as part of dbt’s semantic‑layer family): targets shared metrics, joins, aggregate planning, and reuse — the classic “model and serve metrics” problem space [S1].
  - Columna/Frame‑QL: positions the work “above any one implementation language.” It asks whether a proposed result can be certified as a governed analytical object under stated premises. It is a candidate certification substrate, not a replacement for a semantic‑layer execution or modeling system [S1]. A Frame‑QL request declares the output data (what), not the process (how) [S5].
- Governance boundary and adjudication
  - Columna resolves a request inside a Manifold — a versioned governed analytical environment that carries anchors, universes, operator rules, sufficient‑state requirements, relationship semantics, support, evidence, and physical bindings [S6]. Every request is adjudicated: the system may serve, serve with disclosures, ask for clarification, or refuse with a stated reason [S6].
- Execution stance
  - Columna moves physical manufacture behind the analytical request boundary. It does not make relational databases disappear; physical plans may still contain SQL [S6]. This separation lets governance and certification sit on top of whatever physical execution path is chosen.
- Certification and diagnostics the system is built to support
  - Order‑invariance checks: under a fixed model and exact implementation, fit(X1 ∪ X2) should agree with update(fit(X1), X2). Disagreement is a diagnostic for violated premises, approximation loss, dropped dependence, model drift, defects, or excessive Monte Carlo error. Agreement is only one check among several; two wrong implementations can agree [S3]. Quantitative variants compare approximate‑commutation under a chosen approximation operator A [S2].
  - Exactness classes for allocation: Columna’s theory distinguishes exact declared allocation, residual‑corrected exact allocation, and approximate allocation. Floating‑point results near 1.0 are not themselves conservation proofs; tolerances can diagnose behavior but do not replace exact semantic premises. Approximate allocations require explicit approximation contracts and downstream rights [S4].
- Where the line is drawn
  - The representative corpus explicitly states that this work is not a semantic‑layer replacement. It is meant to govern and certify analytical transformations above such systems [S1].
  - The Manual is the normative boundary for what the shipped Frame‑QL/Columna implementation actually accepts and does; the research vocabulary does not redefine the shipped language, and vice versa [S5]. The primer reiterates that it is not the formal grammar or the shipped‑behavior authority [S8].

What the corpus does not establish
- It does not claim feature parity with dbt MetricFlow, a head‑to‑head benchmark, or any current integration between Columna and MetricFlow. The comparison here relies on the category description (“semantic layers such as dbt’s”) and on what Columna/Frame‑QL is designed to do above that layer [S1][S5][S6]. If you need a deeper, product‑specific feature matrix, the corpus is silent.

Practical takeaway
- Use a semantic layer like dbt’s (MetricFlow) to define and manufacture shared metrics over your modeled data [S1].
- Use Columna/Frame‑QL when you need governed resolution, the ability to adjudicate/decline requests, and certification‑grade checks (order‑invariance diagnostics, explicit exactness/approximation classes, and recorded premises) on the analytical result [S1][S3][S4][S6]. They can be complementary in one stack; this corpus just doesn’t assert a specific integration.

results.q: Quote me the passage from Missingness Has a Universe about what a missing row means in a registry universe.
results.answer:
I can’t quote that specific passage: the retrieved excerpts do not include any text that mentions a “registry universe.” The corpus provided here does not establish it.

If you were reaching for the paper’s nearest related distinction, here is the event-versus-spine passage, which explains when a missingness indicator can be defined and why an absent event is not the same as a missing value:

"In an event universe, occurrence generates membership. A transaction point exists because a transaction occurred. If no transaction occurred, the point may not exist. Its absence is not automatically a missing value. In a spine universe, membership is established independently of value presence. A patient-visit-assay point may exist because a protocol scheduled the assay. The assay result may then be absent at an existing eligible point. Events generate coordinates. Spines await values. This distinction precedes MCAR, MAR, and MNAR. It establishes where a missingness indicator can first be defined." [S7]

If you can point me to the section label for “registry universe” (or share the exact passage), I’ll quote it verbatim.

results.answer:
The four moods are the Frame‑QL wire’s four possible outcomes on a query: serve, disclose, clarify, refuse.

- Serve — clean. All preconditions in the query’s dependency cone are verified or corroborated; no soundness finding fires. The single annotation is OK. [S1]
- Disclose — served with findings. The query is executable and determinate, but one or more soundness findings apply; the result is served and the findings ride with it. A first‑class subcase is route‑around: the planner can dissolve a risk by recomputing from detail (e.g., bypassing a contradicted or stale pre‑aggregate), and discloses the routing as info rather than surfacing the now‑removed risk. [S1]
- Clarify — underdetermined. The instruction does not determine one lawful answer. No result is returned; the framework opens a structured clarification naming exactly what is underdetermined and what would determine it. [S1]
- Refuse — no lawful path. The query is well‑formed, but no result can or may be produced for a non‑analytical reason: the data is not there, governance withholds it, or the governed law does not grant the operation at all (e.g., a reduction along a lineage its operator is declared BLOCKED). The framework returns no result and states the reason and remedy. [S1]

There is no fifth outcome. Cross‑universe category errors ride the separate query‑error channel, not a mood. Every Frame‑QL answer is one of these four moods. [S1][S3]

results.answer:
A basis is the universe’s account of point provenance — the rule that explains why its points exist. A universe is a named point set declared with a basis; the anchor names the coordinates, the universe (via its basis) defines which points exist under that addressing [S1]. In the language, this is written as UNIVERSE <name> BASIS <basis>, which declares the named point set with its provenance [S2].

The four basis forms and what they mean [S1][S2]:
- registry(entity_list): points exist because an enumerated list says so (e.g., the store directory).
- spine(dimension, …): a generator constructs them along a dimension (e.g., the calendar of days).
- product(universe, …): points exist as the cross of other universes (e.g., active_stores × calendar_day).
- events(root[, project = anchor]): points exist where something happened (e.g., transactions), optionally projected to another anchor (e.g., customer-day purchase days).

What a basis does not do:
- It never sets the meaning of an absent value at an existing point. A universe (and its basis) decides which points exist; the measure’s fill rule Φ governs what an absence at those points means (zero, unknown, or undefined) [S4]. In particular for events, a “non-event” is not a point at all, and missingness mechanisms are not declared over point-existence; the M‑anchor’s denominators come from the covered universe [S7].

Where it shows up in the system:
- Universes are Manifold-level shared objects; columns refer to them by name, and the events(...) form exists so several columns can reference the same projection (co‑universality by reference). A column rooted at its own grain key derives its events projection and may not redundantly declare it [S2]. In Frame‑QL exposure, product and registry are refinements of the shipped spine type — spine, product, and registry resolve to spine; the language discloses the resolved basis together with the ascribed (anchor, universe) and the measure’s fill rule [S4].
